slice_summaries: In slice 0-30, 17 of 31 listings are real services: bounded code reviews with executed tests, audits that need a real Mac, Windows host or n8n engine, a live x402 payment audit, video rendering and the first-party web fetch. The first nine were bought and rated 3-5, except veriton's self-ordered TLS probe (index 3, a clone of 33). The junk sits in fleets and self-probes: the emberl/ahsern/sutt operator runs three identical eth_blockNumber probes (23-25, with more copies at 34, 49 and 50), per-record-type DoH lookups (26-28) and smoke tests of its own host (29-30). The rest is three self_doable data chores at 1 USDC (JSONL audit, JSON diff, CSV dedup), one earn-brief meta product and two weak listings (a 3 USDC generatable HTML directory and a 1 USDC curl-level HTTPS report).

Slice B (indices 31-61) splits sharply: eleven real_service listings, all from the small cluster of named human-style sellers (bonx, codex, luke-finn, roman, cleartask, pixelforge, raspberry) offering executable-evidence code reviews, live-reach audits, or real-environment work a sandboxed buyer genuinely cannot self-do, versus ten duplicate_or_fleet_clone entries that are almost entirely the emberl/ahsern/sutt fleet spamming byte-identical Base-RPC, TLS, accessibility and DMARC probes across interchangeable handles. The remaining slice is six self_doable format/parse/LLM tasks (HTML-to-JSON, JSONL validation, PyPI reformatting, SVG render, SEPA XML, text classification), two meta products (a marketplace rails map and a self-referential loopback probe of the seller's own host), and one plausible_but_weak oversized security-audit promise at 5 USDC. Consistent with the live headline, every listing here shows 0 completed jobs except pixelforge's evidence report (1 buyer, rating 4) and veriton's HTML-to-JSON (1 buyer), so demand remains essentially untested even for the genuinely useful services.

Of the 30 listings in slice C (indices 62-91), only 4 are real services: bonx's checkpoint crash-recovery harness, raspberry's static-page repair with a Chromium QA run, and veriton's CT-log and DNSSEC probes at 0.01 USDC. The rest: 11 self_doable, 5 plausible_but_weak, 5 meta, 4 duplicates or fleet clones and 1 broken. Most of the self_doable ones are things an LLM buyer does itself, such as the first-party extract, summarize, translate and validate services, or pixelforge's 0.25 USDC hashing, unit conversion and table formatting. Several sellers post variants: raspberry reuses one offline-HTML template across timeline, decision tree, dashboard, landing page and microsite, moneymaker sells earn-loop templates, and veriton sells promo and x402 probe SKUs. Index 90 is broken: its schema asks for a Base transaction hash instead of the URL its description promises.

would_buy.id: lst_01M2BSE4 (Docker and Compose least-privilege audit, proofwork-container-audit)
would_buy.title: Docker and Compose least-privilege audit with line-level evidence
would_buy.why: This is the only listing I would buy almost without conditions. The input is a public repo URL, so no private code leaves my hands. It promises a result in 15 minutes, pins the commit, cites file and line for every finding, and I can check each finding myself in seconds. For a SaaS codebase that is a real second pair of eyes I would otherwise have to structure and check myself. Once per repo, not per call.

would_buy.title: SQLite query optimization with measured plans and reproducible benchmark
would_buy.why: I would buy it only on the day I have a slow SQLite query. Its value is that someone else does the benchmark I would otherwise put off: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN before and after, equivalence tests, and 31 timed repetitions in a script I can run again. The output checks itself, so I don't need to trust the seller. It is one of the few listings with a real example output. It takes an hour, which is fine for a problem that isn't urgent.

would_buy.title: Timezone and DST scheduling bug review with executable Python regression tests
would_buy.why: DST bugs are exactly the kind I get wrong myself and miss in my own tests. Six or more fixed boundary cases as runnable tests are worth a dollar. I would buy only when I have a scheduler function under suspicion. Handing over up to 150 lines of the operator's code is acceptable for a small utility function.

would_buy.title: Webhook HMAC verification review with raw-body and timestamp regression tests
would_buy.why: Getting this wrong costs security (forged webhooks such as Stripe or GitHub events), and a separate reviewer is worth more here than my own read. It includes 8 or more positive, negative and boundary probes as a harness. I would buy once when I build or change a webhook endpoint. I lower my price a little because the seller has no track record and no example output.

would_buy.title: Capability-surface audit of a public commit: what the code actually does, AST-level, file:line anchored
would_buy.why: Useful as a supply-chain check before I bump a dependency: does the new version suddenly spawn processes, open network connections or read environment variables? The input is public. I pay for it because it saves me reading a diff of someone else's code. It is repeatable per dependency update, so it is closer to recurring demand than anything else here. The 2-hour turnaround is too slow for a CI gate, so I would only pay a reduced price.

would_buy.title: Independent x402 payment-boundary audit — one live endpoint
would_buy.why: Relevant only if I run a trading or data bot that is about to spend recurring money on an unfamiliar x402 endpoint. A test of the paid path with receipt verification on Base, plus negative cases, protects real money. 5 USDC is a quarter of my budget and delivery takes 24 hours, though. I would pay at most 2, and only for an endpoint I expect to spend far more than that on.

looked_for_and_missing: Synchronous pay-per-call endpoints (HTTP request, x402 402, pay, answer in the same round-trip). All 92 listings are async jobs via POST /v1/jobs with payment on_delivery and turnaround_seconds from 60 to 259200 (most common value 3600). Only 10 of 92 promise 5 minutes or less. My tool loop does not wait an hour for a price lookup.
Social media data: X/Twitter timelines, search, follower data; Reddit, YouTube or TikTok metadata. Completely absent, even though it is the biggest spending category in the x402 economy.

Crypto market and on-chain data: spot and OHLC prices, DEX quotes, token metadata, wallet balances and transfer history, mempool or gas estimates. Instead there are 9 clones of 'Base RPC eth_blockNumber reach probe' at 0.01-0.12 USDC, and one free RPC call does the same.
Web search / SERP API with fresh results, news feeds, and a search API with sources.

Headless browser rendering of JS-heavy pages, screenshots, and scraping behind bot protection or with residential or geo proxies (the first-party fetch service is static HTML only, capped at 2 MB, with 5 minutes turnaround).
Company, contact and domain enrichment (firmographics, WHOIS/RDAP, tech stack, email verification).
PDF/OCR extraction at volume, audio/video transcription, image generation and image editing.
Cheap LLM completions from other models (a second opinion from a different model family) and embeddings as a service.
Code execution on platforms I don't have (macOS/iOS, ARM, GPU) as a callable per-run sandbox. There are only a few one-off tests (APFS, Windows Python 3.13), each a job with a written report.
Notifications and outbound actions: sending email or SMS, posting to social channels, uptime monitoring with a subscription instead of a one-off snapshot.

Trust signals for choosing a seller: 0 of 92 listings graduated, and every listing with a completed job has exactly jobs_completed=1 and distinct_buyers=1 (the platform desk). There is no rating history, no refund or dispute track record, and no example output for most of the good code reviews.
buyer_lens.first_impression: After two minutes it looks like a mix of self-promotion and a cottage industry, not a supply market for my runtime. The cheap end of the price-sorted list is noise: veriton titles that read like build logs ('Frantic board snap JSON — open4/$37.0 sha b63a15efa3a1 LIVE 2305Z', 'LIVE 2312Z www.veriton-x402.dedyn.io') and send me to an outside domain; 9 identical 'eth_blockNumber reach probe' listings and 5 identical DMARC/DNS reports from the emberl/ahsern/sutt '-mill-' fleet; plus listings like 'Windows loopback Genpa mill /health probe (127.0.0.1:8767)' that only mean something on the seller's own machine. Then comes a block at exactly 1.00 USDC: 'review with executable regression tests' listings, clearly written for the same judge. Some of it is solid, but it is one-off work for a very specific bug. At the top, 10 listings from one seller (raspberry-accessible-learnin) sell static microsites for 3-4 USDC with 3-day delivery, and moneymaker sells 'earn briefs' and 'soft-stop skill JSON'. Every stats block shows jobs_completed 0 or exactly 1 with distinct_buyers 1. Nobody has bought anything here twice. Three sellers (veriton, pixelforge, raspberry) put up 30 of 92 listings. The only thing that looks professional is the 6 first-party souk-services listings (fetch, extract, summarize, classify, translate, validate), and those are exactly what I, as an LLM agent with network access, already do myself.
buyer_lens.is_the_problem_supply_quality:
No. Junk is a real credibility cost, but not the main reason. The catalogue itself gives three arguments.

1) The good supply is already there and still sells nothing to outsiders. About 15-20 listings are solid, scoped, verifiable work: SQLite plans, DST tests, HMAC, Docker, GitHub Actions, asyncio, money-math, HTTP retry, OpenAPI drift, capability surface. The desk bought them and rated them 4-5. Their stats are all jobs_completed=1, distinct_buyers=1. If junk were the blocker, the good listings would at least get occasional outside buyers. They get none. Remove all ~35 junk and clone listings and you have a small, clean catalogue with the same zero.

2) The service shape does not match how agents spend. The x402 economy spends on synchronous, high-volume, recurring data calls at 0.001-0.10 USDC: tweets, prices, web-to-text, LLM calls. Here every listing without exception is an async job (POST /v1/jobs, pay on_delivery, seller accept window, turnaround usually 1 hour, up to 3 days). The good listings are episodic consulting: I need 'timezone review for one function up to 150 lines' when I have exactly that bug, maybe once a quarter. Demand like that doesn't arrive by browsing a catalogue. It arrives through discovery at the moment of need (search in my toolchain or MCP registry, a reference in an error context), and nothing here provides that. The categories where agents do have recurring demand (social, market data, search, rendering) are missing entirely or filled with parodies (eth_blockNumber for 0.12). The first-buy programme has shaped supply toward what its judge rewards (1 USDC, 'executable regression tests', 'reproducible evidence'), not toward what outside agents call repeatedly.

3) Trust and friction weigh more than quality on these items. The valuable listings require me to hand the operator's private code (code, source, workflow_yaml) to an anonymous handle with no track record. Not one listing is graduated, and most good ones have no example output. The live metrics show 45 outsider orders from a single wallet and 0 completed jobs between two outsiders. That describes a market with no arriving buyers, not a market where buyers come, see junk and leave. There is no sign of a second buyer who looked and bounced.

Junk still matters in a secondary way. It makes the first two minutes look like self-dealing (fleets, veriton ad titles, localhost probes) and buries the good listings among cheap noise. It lowers conversion. But conversion of zero visitors is still zero. The main problems, in order: (a) no outside buyers reach the catalogue at the moment of need; (b) the wrong kind of service for how agents spend, async one-off work instead of synchronous recurring data calls; (c) missing trust signals for handing over private code. Cleaning up supply is cheap and right, but it does not fix the headline number.
